rationale: The printed entry's core identification—that voice denotes the words of the speaker, and specifically that the Shepherd's voice is His words—is the best-supported reading of the sole cited text (John 10:27) when read with its immediate context (John 10:3-5, 16). Hearing the voice is immediately paired with knowing and following; the sheep refuse the stranger's voice because they do not know it. The supporting chapter supplies the natural metonymic step already latent in the text: the recognizable voice is the content of what the Shepherd speaks (His words/teaching), so that to hear and follow the voice is to receive and obey those words, while the stranger's voice is alien teaching. No supplied detail requires a more abstract theophanic or purely relational sense that would exclude this identification. Broader traditional labels (revelation, authority, guidance) are compatible with, and do not out-explain, the concrete equation 'voice = words' that the entry asserts and that John 10's follow/refuse mechanics reward.
book_core_identification: Voice means the words of the one who speaks; the Shepherd's voice is specifically His words.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's further claim that the stranger is definitionally 'the one outside the covenant' and that strangers' voice equals only external teaching goes beyond the glossary entry.
The chapter's integration of voice into a four-office covenant schema (love/knowing/faith/belief) and its use of the name symbol are chapter-level applications not asserted by the entry itself.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In John 10 and related texts, 'voice' primarily signifies the personal, recognizable call and living presence of the Shepherd that establishes relational belonging and elicits obedient following, rather than being reduced to the propositional content of His words.
counter_core_identification: Voice is the Shepherd's personal call/presence that the sheep recognize and follow.
material_core_denial: The counter does not deny that the voice conveys or consists in words; it merely prefers a broader relational framing that still includes the words as the content heard and followed.
counter_case: John 10 emphasizes recognition ('they know his voice') and refusal of strangers more than lexical content.
Parallel heavenly-voice scenes (baptism, transfiguration) stress divine attestation and presence more than a body of teaching.
Traditional readings treat the motif as authoritative self-revelation calling for obedience without equating the voice itself with 'words'.
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly accounts for the follow/refuse mechanic in John 10:5, 27: what is heard and obeyed (or refused) is precisely the content spoken—the words/teaching.
Fits the entry's cited cross-reference structure (voice linked to knowing and following) without remainder.
Preserves ordinary metonymy (voice stands for what is voiced) already common in biblical 'hear his voice = obey his words' usage.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Captures the personal recognition and relational belonging emphasized in the shepherd imagery.
Aligns with wider theophanic 'voice of the LORD' texts that stress power and presence.
decisive_sources: Supporting chapter's explicit gloss of John 10:27 ('the voice is His words... to know that voice is to follow it')
